classification.difficultyReason: Identify shaded equal parts, including three triangular eighths, then apply the taught fraction-to-percentage conversion.

questions.mappingNote: Apply parts-per-hundred meaning to hundred grids and equivalent fractions to tenths and eighths.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 models percentages using hundred grids; pages 2–4 convert equivalent fractions to percentages.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify shaded proportions using hundredths, tenths and eighths.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert fractions with denominators 10, 100 and 1000 directly to percentages.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess fraction-to-percentage conversion. Parts a–d already have denominator 100, e–f require scaling by 10, and g–h require dividing numerator and denominator by 10. Page 5 was inspected for the exercise context; its exact fractional-percentage examples are unnecessary for these terminating results.
questions.methodNote: Write an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, then express its numerator as a percentage. Page 4 Example 3(a,b) supplies the directly referenced method; pages 2–3 explain percentages as parts per hundred and equivalent fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert fractions with denominators 10, 100 and 1000 directly to percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate taught conversion from each supplied representation to fill the other two labelled rows, simplifying fractions where needed.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 combines the conversion methods demonstrated on pages 2–4 in a three-row equivalence table. Page 5 establishes exact fractional percentages where necessary, although every value here terminates.
questions.methodNote: Write percentages over 100 and simplify; use decimal place value and equivalent fractions; multiply a fraction or decimal by 100% to express it as a percentage.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete equivalent forms using terminating decimals, simple fractions and percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert fractions to percentages, retaining exact mixed fractional percentages for non-terminating values.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts directly assess fraction-to-percentage conversion. Example 5 explicitly retains exact fractional percentages; its part b uses the same fraction as question 9e.
questions.methodNote: Multiply the fraction by 100%, then simplify the numerical coefficient to an exact mixed number, following Example 5 on PDF page 5. Pages 2–4 establish percentages and the multiplication rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert fractions to percentages, retaining exact mixed fractional percentages for non-terminating values.

classification.difficultyReason: Expresses quantities as percentages after converting to common units, including squared units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expresses quantities as percentages after converting to common units, including squared units.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct calculations using familiar equivalent fractions, including one eighth, one third and two fifths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct calculations using familiar equivalent fractions, including one eighth, one third and two fifths.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the relevant percentages from a shared context, calculate two quantities and find the remaining percentage.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the relevant percentages from a shared context, calculate two quantities and find the remaining percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Write ordered ratios directly from two given counts, adding the counts for the whole.

Example 11 models ordered family-count ratios; Example 12 explains equal parts. Example 11(c) has a printed numerical error: seven females out of ten people gives 7:10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Write ordered ratios directly from two given counts, adding the counts for the whole.

Page 10 introduces ordered comparisons; page 11 Examples 11–12 use ordered category counts and equal parts; page 12 explains simplification by a common factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count coloured shapes, preserve the requested comparison order and simplify the resulting ratios.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide both terms of each whole-number ratio by their highest common factor.
